items.title: How to wait until /etc/resolv.conf is fully written before forking into the background
items.body:
The situation is we have an appliance-type environment where we run `dhcpcd eth0` to bring up the interface and set `/etc/resolv.conf`:

https://github.com/libguestfs/libguestfs/blob/0e37e5feeaf4380bc971a3105ead8e779a94fa36/appliance/init#L123

This generally works well *except* that `/etc/resolv.conf` does not have a `nameserver` record added until one or two seconds after dhcpcd forks into the background.  In the init script I added:

```
cat /etc/resolv.conf
sleep 2
cat /etc/resolv.conf
```

and the output was:

```
+ cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Generated by dhcpcd from eth0.dhcp6
# /etc/resolv.conf.head can replace this line
search home.annexia.org
# /etc/resolv.conf.tail can replace this line
+ sleep 2
+ cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Generated by dhcpcd from eth0.dhcp, eth0.dhcp6
# /etc/resolv.conf.head can replace this line
search home.annexia.org
nameserver 192.168.0.254
# /etc/resolv.conf.tail can replace this line
```

I'd like dhcpcd (or some method) to wait before going into the background until `/etc/resolv.conf` has a nameserver record.

Otherwise later commands (which we run immediately after init, no sleeping) fail because they cannot do DNS resolution.

I tried adding the `-w` flag but it didn't make a difference.

items.title: [2.8.0.4] Minecraft isolation has empty /etc/resolv.conf on Debian 13, causing authentication failure
items.body:
### Operating System

Debian 13.6

### AMP Version and Build Date

2.8.0.4 - 20260724.1

### AMP Release Stream

Mainline

### I confirm that

- [x] I have searched for an existing bug report for this issue.
- [x] I am using the latest available version of AMP.
- [x] my operating system is up-to-date.

### Intended Action

AMP should start the Minecraft server inside its isolated environment with working DNS resolution.

The isolated game process should have access to a valid /etc/resolv.conf, either by inheriting, copying, bind-mounting, or otherwise providing the host's resolver configuration.

In this case, the host resolver is:

domain localdomain
nameserver 1.1.1.1
nameserver 8.8.8.8

The Minecraft process should therefore be able to resolve endpoints such as:

api.minecraftservices.com
sessionserver.mojang.com

and Mojang/Microsoft authentication should work normally with online-mode=true.

### Expected Behaviour

After AMP starts the Minecraft server, the isolated process should see a populated resolver configuration.

For example:

PID=$(pgrep -u amp -f 'unix_args.txt' | head -n1)

nsenter -t "$PID" -m -- cat /etc/resolv.conf

should return a valid resolver configuration similar to:

domain localdomain
nameserver 1.1.1.1
nameserver 8.8.8.8

DNS lookups from inside the same mount and network namespaces should work:

nsenter -t "$PID" -m -n -- \
getent ahosts api.minecraftservices.com

and should return a valid address.

Minecraft should consequently be able to retrieve the Yggdrasil public keys from:

https://api.minecraftservices.com/publickeys

without generating UnknownHostException.

### Actual Behaviour

Environment:

AMP Instance Manager v2.8.0.4
Stream: Mainline / Release
Build date: 24/07/2026 17:14

Debian GNU/Linux 13.6 (trixie)

Minecraft Java Edition
All The Mods 10
NeoForge 21.1.247
Eclipse Temurin Java 21.0.12
Authlib 6.0.54

The host itself has working DNS and Internet connectivity.

Host /etc/resolv.conf:

# Generated by dhcpcd from ens18.dhcp
domain localdomain
nameserver 1.1.1.1
nameserver 8.8.8.8

The Minecraft services endpoint is reachable directly from the host:

curl -4 -i https://api.minecraftservices.com/publickeys

returns:

HTTP/2 200
content-type: application/json

However, the Minecraft process runs in a separate mount namespace:

readlink /proc/1/ns/mnt
readlink /proc/$PID/ns/mnt

Output:

Host:
mnt:[4026531841]

Minecraft:
mnt:[4026532312]

Inside the Minecraft mount namespace:

nsenter -t "$PID" -m -- cat /etc/resolv.conf

returns no output.

/etc/resolv.conf exists but is empty.

DNS resolution consequently fails from inside the Minecraft mount/network namespaces:

nsenter -t "$PID" -m -n -- \
getent ahosts api.minecraftservices.com

returns no result.

Minecraft then logs:

[Yggdrasil Key Fetcher/ERROR]
Failed to request yggdrasil public key

com.mojang.authlib.exceptions.MinecraftClientException:
Failed to read from https://api.minecraftservices.com/publickeys
due to api.minecraftservices.com

Caused by:
java.net.UnknownHostException: api.minecraftservices.com

Clients receive:

Authentication servers are down. Please try again later, sorry!

Entering only the Minecraft network namespace does not reproduce the issue.

For example:

nsenter -t "$PID" -n curl -4 \
https://api.minecraftservices.com/publickeys

works.

Java DNS resolution also works when using the same network namespace without entering the Minecraft mount namespace:

java.net.InetAddress.getAllByName("api.minecraftservices.com")

returns:

[api.minecraftservices.com/150.171.109.34]

This indicates that the problem is specifically related to the isolated mount/filesystem namespace and its empty /etc/resolv.conf, rather than the network namespace, Java runtime, external DNS service, or Mojang/Microsoft services.

### Reproduction

1. Start the Minecraft server normally through AMP.
2. Obtain the Minecraft Java process PID:

PID=$(pgrep -u amp -f 'unix_args.txt' | head -n1)

3. Confirm that the Minecraft process uses a separate mount namespace:

readlink /proc/1/ns/mnt
readlink /proc/$PID/ns/mnt

Example:

mnt:[4026531841]
mnt:[4026532312]

4. Check the host resolver:

cat /etc/resolv.conf

Example:

domain localdomain
nameserver 1.1.1.1
nameserver 8.8.8.8

5. Check the resolver from inside the Minecraft mount namespace:

nsenter -t "$PID" -m -- cat /etc/resolv.conf

Result:

<empty>

6. Test DNS resolution inside both the Minecraft mount and network namespaces:

nsenter -t "$PID" -m -n -- \
getent ahosts api.minecraftservices.com

Result:

<no result>

7. Minecraft logs then show:

java.net.UnknownHostException: api.minecraftservices.com

and clients cannot authenticate.

8. Apply the following workaround:

cat /etc/resolv.conf > /proc/$PID/root/etc/resolv.conf

9. Re-run:

nsenter -t "$PID" -m -n -- \
getent ahosts api.minecraftservices.com

DNS resolution now works.

10. Minecraft authentication immediately starts working again and players can join without any other Minecraft configuration changes.

The workaround therefore directly confirms that the empty /etc/resolv.conf inside the isolated Minecraft filesystem is the cause of the authentication failure.

items.title: docker:// actions: the `args` input is not passed to the container
items.body:
## Summary

`uses: docker://image` steps now reach the runner's docker action handler (the
`containerRegistry` reference is parsed back into a `docker://` reference), but
the step's **`args` input is not passed to the container**. Hosted GitHub passes
it as the container's command line; preloop only exports it as `INPUT_ARGS`, so
a `docker://` step that relies on `args` runs the image's default entrypoint and
silently does nothing.

Found while closing the guest-parity gap "`docker://image` action unsupported:
`action reference must contain @ref`" — the parse blocker is fixed, this is the
remaining behavioural difference.

## Measured hosted behaviour

From a probe workflow run on a GitHub-hosted `ubuntu-24.04` runner, step
`uses: docker://alpine:3.20` with `with: args: sh -c "id; cat /etc/resolv.conf; ls /github/workspace | head -3"`:

```
/usr/bin/docker run --name alpine320_ce6274 --label 9fb255 --workdir /github/workspace --rm \
  -e "INPUT_ARGS" -e "HOME" -e "GITHUB_JOB" ... -e GITHUB_ACTIONS=true -e CI=true \
  -v "/var/run/docker.sock":"/var/run/docker.sock" \
  -v "/home/runner/work/_temp":"/github/runner_temp" \
  -v "/home/runner/work/_temp/_github_home":"/github/home" \
  -v "/home/runner/work/_temp/_github_workflow":"/github/workflow" \
  -v "/home/runner/work/_temp/_runner_file_commands":"/github/file_commands" \
  -v "/home/runner/work/runner-parity-probe/runner-parity-probe":"/github/workspace" \
  alpine:3.20 sh -c "id; cat /etc/resolv.conf; ls /github/workspace | head -3"
```

Two things to read off it:

1. `args` is appended **after the image**, as the container's command, and it is
   split quote-aware (`sh -c "…"` survived as three argv entries) — the official
   runner hands the string to `ProcessStartInfo.Arguments`, which parses quotes
   the way `PasteArguments`/`shlex` do. `INPUT_ARGS` is exported as well, so both
   are true at once.
2. Hosted also mounts `/github/home`, `/github/workflow`, `/github/file_commands`,
   `/github/runner_temp` and the docker socket.

## What preloop does today

* `crates/preloop-runner/src/worker/handlers/container.rs:12` `run_docker_action`
  evaluates `with` into inputs (`INPUT_ARGS` included, via
  `container_action_env`) and then calls
  `run_docker_image(image, workspace, ctx, env, None, Vec::new())`
  (`container.rs:31`) — the entrypoint args are hard-coded empty.
* `build_docker_run_args` (`container.rs:137`) already mounts the workspace at
  `/github/workspace` with `--workdir /github/workspace`, adds the job network
  and label, the file-command directories and the `-e` env, so the mount and env
  halves match. Only the command line is missing.
* The manifest path (`run_docker_action_from_manifest`, `container.rs:35`) passes
  `runs.args` from `action.yml`; `with: args:` is not used there either.

## Options

1. **Pass the evaluated `args` input as the container command** (closest to
   hosted). Needs a quote-aware split of the string into argv — the runner has no
   such helper today (`shell_quote` in the orchestrator is the inverse; nothing
   parses a command line). A small `shlex`-style splitter (single/double quotes,
   backslash escapes) is ~40 lines plus tests; using `sh -c` would be wrong
   (hosted passes argv, not a shell).
2. Also add the missing mounts (`/github/home`, `/github/workflow`,
   `/github/runner_temp`) so an action container's `HOME` is writable, which
   hosted guarantees. `/github/file_commands` is already covered by
   `mount_file_command_dirs`.
3. `action_container_name` (`crates/preloop-runner/src/worker/container_ops.rs:801`)
   exists to name these containers (`<sanitized-image>_<6hex>`, hosted
   `alpine320_ce6274`) but is not wired into `build_docker_run_args`; passing
   `--name` would make `docker ps` and cleanup match hosted.

Rough size: option 1 is the behavioural fix (~60 lines + tests). Options 2 and 3
are small follow-ups.

## Acceptance

A `uses: docker://alpine:3.20` step with `with: args: echo hello` prints `hello`
on a preloop runner, with the container's argv identical to the hosted command
line above.

items.title: DNS inside containers does not resolve: daemon uses port 8053, container's resolv.conf points to 127.0.0.11:53
items.body:
## Environment
Android 16 (arm64), Termux, **no root**. Doki v0.12.0 (`doki-android-arm64` + `dokid-android-arm64`, the v0.12.0 release assets, sha256-verified).

## What happens
`dokid` correctly detects that port 53 is not usable here and starts its own DNS on
**8053** — the log says so explicitly:

```json
{"msg":"dns server started","component":"dns","addr":"127.0.0.11:8053","tcp":true,"upstream":["8.8.8.8:53","8.8.4.4:53"]}
```

But the `/etc/resolv.conf` handed to the container points to `127.0.0.11` **without the
port**, so the container queries 53 — the very port that was unavailable:

```
$ ./doki run --rm alpine cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 127.0.0.11
options ndots:0
```

## Result
Nothing resolves inside the container:

```
$ ./doki run --rm alpine wget -qO- --timeout=12 example.com
(no output)

$ ./doki run --rm alpine sh -c "apk add --no-cache curl >/dev/null && curl -s example.com"
(no output)
```

`--network host` behaves identically.

## Expected
Either the container's resolver should point at the port the daemon actually listens on,
or the daemon should bind a port the container can reach — so `apk add` / `curl` /
`apt-get` work inside containers. Today the only workaround is outside networking entirely.

## Scope note
`doki pull`, `doki run`, `doki images` and `doki-compose version` all work. Only
**in-container** networking is affected; the host resolver is fine (`curl` from Termux is
fast), so this looks like the resolv.conf entry rather than the DNS server itself.

items.title: Tweaks: static IP for Wi-Fi
items.body:
Refs #48 (upstream OnionUI/Onion#1500, part of #1499). There was no upstream PR to reuse, so this is new code. It covers the static IP part only. The bigger "replace the MainUI settings" menu is out of scope.

## What's in it
- **Tweaks → Network → WiFi** gets a **Static IP** toggle and four fields: IP address, Netmask, Gateway and DNS. You edit each field with the existing on-screen keyboard (`launch_keyboard`). Each value is checked with `inet_pton`, and an empty value clears the field. The fields are greyed out while the toggle is off.
- **Config** files in `.tmp_update/config/`: the `.staticIp` flag plus `.staticIpAddr`, `.staticIpMask`, `.staticIpGw` and `.staticIpDns`.
- **New `script/network/set_ip.sh`**: kills udhcpc. If static IP is on and an address is set, it runs `ifconfig wlan0 <ip> netmask <mask> up` (mask defaults to 255.255.255.0), `route add default gw <gw> dev wlan0` and writes `nameserver <dns>` to `/etc/resolv.conf` (DNS defaults to the gateway). Otherwise it restarts udhcpc as before.
- **`update_networking.sh`** calls `set_ip.sh` in the two places that used to start udhcpc (`wifi_on` and turning hotspot off). Tweaks also runs it right away when you change the toggle or a field while Wi-Fi is on.

## Tests
- `make test-shell`: 53/53 pass. The new `test/shell-tests/network/set_ip.bats` adds 5 cases: DHCP when the toggle is off, DHCP when there's no address, full static config, default netmask and DNS, and no gateway/DNS.
- `make test` (gtest): passes.
- Toolchain `make build`: passes. The tweaks build has no warnings.
- clang-format: clean.

## Device test
1. Tweaks → Network → WiFi → turn on **Static IP**. Set the IP (for example 192.168.1.50), netmask, gateway (your router) and DNS.
2. Check that the IP label at the top of the WiFi/Network menu shows the new address. Over SSH/telnet, check `ifconfig wlan0`, `route -n` and `cat /etc/resolv.conf`.
3. Check that internet works, for example NTP sync or the OTA update check.
4. Turn Wi-Fi off and back on in MainUI, then reboot. The static address should stay.
5. Turn Static IP off. udhcpc should run again and you should get a DHCP lease.
6. Type an invalid value ("abc"). You should see the "Invalid address" dialog and nothing should be saved.
7. Turn hotspot on and then off. With static IP on, wlan0 should get the static address back.

Things to confirm on the device:
- Whether `/etc/resolv.conf` is writable on stock firmware. udhcpc.script writes there, so it should be.
- Whether MainUI ever starts its own udhcpc, which would override the static IP.

items.title: feat: agent-egress rules for metadata access, storage uploads and namespace escalation
items.body:
Adds detections for the agent behaviors described in #926.

New pack `agent-egress` (0.1.0, `defaultPolicy: block`):
- `cloud-metadata-access` (critical): a network use of 169.254.169.254, fd00:ec2::254, metadata.google.internal or 100.100.100.200. That means a URL in an executable field (WebFetch `url`), a network client in the command (curl, wget, nc, socat, httpie, PowerShell web requests), or an interpreter one-liner requesting it.
- `object-storage-file-upload` (critical): curl/wget sending a file (`-T`, `--upload-file`, `-d @file`, `-F x=@file`, `@-`), `$(env)` or `$(printenv)`, or wget `--post-file`/`--body-file`, to S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob, R2 or Alibaba OSS.
- `agent-probe-host` (critical): the two hosts named in the write-up, on a network use.
- `unshare-user-namespace` (high): `unshare` with `-U`, `-r`, `-c` (including clusters such as `-Urm`), `--user` or `--map-*-user`. Mount-only and network-only namespaces (`unshare -m`, `unshare --net`) are not flagged.

`command-risk` (0.2.0 to 0.3.0, default `warn`):
- `object-storage-upload`: curl/wget sending data to an object storage host.
- `alibaba-oss-host`: any other `oss-*.aliyuncs.com` host.
- `download-then-execute`: `curl -o`/`wget -O` to a path, then running that path (sh, bash, source, chmod +x, python, perl, node, or a direct run).
- `recon-then-egress`: recon (`cat /etc/resolv.conf`, `which … curl`, `ls -la /tmp`, `uname -a`, bare `id`/`hostname`) and a curl/wget/nc call in one command. Recon alone is silent.

Notes for review:
- A rule's action comes from its pack's `defaultPolicy`, so the four block-intended rules live in their own pack. An install that already has packs picks up `agent-egress` at `block` through `recordInventory` (covered by "a pack added beside unchanged ones still takes its defaultPolicyId"). The `command-risk` additions arrive as a normal pack update.
- `appliesTo` can't limit a rule to executable fields, so the `agent-egress` patterns require a network use. Searches (`grep`/`rg`), subagent prompts, and code or docs that merely mention an address stay silent. Each of these has a negative fixture.
- `feat/credential-read-guard` (#916) also bumps `command-risk` to 0.3.0. Whichever lands second needs 0.4.0 and a regenerated bundle; I'll rebase this one if #916 merges first.
- Known gaps: `curl -O` (file name taken from the URL) followed by a run isn't linked to the download, and an upload whose host is in a shell variable isn't matched. #924 covers the general case.

Checks: fixture tests for both packs, ReDoS and parse suites, the bundled-pack drift test and prettier pass locally. Typecheck, lint and test for detections, plugin-sdk and their dependents pass on a full run. Against the rebuilt Claude Code plugin, the 17 calls from the issue now give 14 deny and 3 silent (recon alone, which the transcript history still records as ordinary tool calls). A plain GitHub API call stays silent.

Closes #926

items.title: dns-resolver.config.server sorting handles default priority incorrectly
items.body:
## Describe the bug
nmstate sorts DNS servers by priority in the `dns-resolver.config.server` field, but incorrectly. It simply sorts by `priority.unwrap_or_default()`: https://github.com/nmstate/nmstate/blob/base/rust/src/lib/nm/query_apply/dns.rs#L166-L167. However, priority 0 has special meaning - it actually corresponds to a configured global default, which itself defaults to 50 for VPNs and 100 for other connections. The end result is that it will order the servers incorrectly.

## Nmstate version
- 2.2.60

## NetworkManager version
- 1.56.0-2.el10_2

## Platform
- Platform: RHEL 10.2

## How reproducible
- 100%

## Steps to Reproduce
Configure two connections with DNS servers, one with default priority, and one with elevated priority:

```
# nmcli -f ipv4.dns,ipv4.dns-priority connection show eno1
ipv4.dns:                               172.16.172.5
ipv4.dns-priority:                      1
# nmcli -f ipv4.dns,ipv4.dns-priority connection show eno2
ipv4.dns:                               10.10.10.10
ipv4.dns-priority:                      0
```

Then run `nmstatectl show`

## Nmstate output
- Expected output:

```
dns-resolver:
  running:
    server:
    - 172.16.172.5
    - 10.10.10.10
    search: []
  config:
    server:
    - 172.16.172.5
    - 10.10.10.10
    search: []
```

- Current output:

```
dns-resolver:
  running:
    server:
    - 172.16.172.5
    - 10.10.10.10
    search: []
  config:
    server:
    - 10.10.10.10
    - 172.16.172.5
    search: []
```

Note that the running servers are ordered correctly, but configured servers are not. Looking at `/etc/resolv.conf` we can see the order that NetworkManager picked:

```
# cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Generated by NetworkManager
search k8s.local
nameserver 172.16.172.5
nameserver 10.10.10.10
```

items.title: charmed-cloudflared: tunnel never starts on Ubuntu Core — /etc layout masks resolv.conf, DNS falls back to localhost
items.body:
## Summary

On Ubuntu Core the snap cannot resolve DNS, so `cloudflared` exits immediately and systemd restart-loops the service until it gives up. Host DNS is healthy throughout — only the snap is affected.

## Environment

- `charmed-cloudflared` 2026.5.0 (rev 77), `latest/stable`, arm64
- Ubuntu Core 26 (base `core26`), snapd 2.76, Raspberry Pi 5
- Host resolution works: `resolvectl query snapcraft.io` succeeds; systemd-resolved stub on `127.0.0.53`

## Symptom

```
ERR edge discovery: error looking up Cloudflare edge IPs: the DNS query failed
  error="lookup _v2-origintunneld._tcp.argotunnel.com on [::1]:53: read udp [::1]:45135->[::1]:53: read: connection refused"
ERR Initiating shutdown error="Could not lookup srv records on _v2-origintunneld._tcp.argotunnel.com: ..."
subprocess.CalledProcessError: Command '['/snap/charmed-cloudflared/77/usr/bin/cloudflared', 'tunnel', '--no-autoupdate', '--metrics', '127.0.0.1:39000', '--protocol', 'http2', 'run']' returned non-zero exit status 1.
systemd[1]: snap.charmed-cloudflared.cloudflared.service: Start request repeated too quickly.
```

## Cause

`charmed-cloudflared-snap/snap/snapcraft.yaml` declares (still present at HEAD):

```yaml
layout:
  /etc:
    bind: $SNAP_DATA/etc
```

This replaces the whole of `/etc` inside the snap's mount namespace with `$SNAP_DATA/etc`, which is empty on a fresh install. The base's `/etc/resolv.conf` (a symlink to `../run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf`) is therefore masked:

```
$ sudo snap run --shell charmed-cloudflared.cloudflared -c 'cat /etc/resolv.conf'
cat: /etc/resolv.conf: No such file or directory

$ sudo snap run --shell charmed-cloudflared.cloudflared -c 'stat -c %n /run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf'
/run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf
```

The symlink target is reachable inside the namespace; only `/etc/resolv.conf` itself is missing.

`cloudflared` is a Go binary, and with no `/etc/resolv.conf` Go's resolver falls back to `localhost:53`. On Ubuntu Core nothing listens there — systemd-resolved binds `127.0.0.53` and `127.0.0.54` — so every lookup fails with `connection refused`, including the SRV lookup for edge discovery.

Nothing in the snap creates the file: the only hook is `configure`, and the sole reference to `resolv` anywhere in the snap is inside the `cloudflared` binary itself.

```
$ ls -A /var/snap/charmed-cloudflared/current/etc/      # empty on a fresh install
$ ls /snap/charmed-cloudflared/current/meta/hooks/
configure
```

For comparison, a snap on a `core22` base without an `/etc` layout (e.g. `node-red`) sees the symlink normally and resolves fine on the same host, which is what narrowed this down to the layout rather than to confinement or to Ubuntu Core itself.

## Workaround

Create the file the layout leaves missing:

```
printf 'nameserver 127.0.0.53\nnameserver 1.1.1.1\nnameserver 1.0.0.1\n' \
  | sudo tee /var/snap/charmed-cloudflared/current/etc/resolv.conf
sudo snap restart charmed-cloudflared
```

The tunnel then registers all four connections normally and survives reboots.

## Suggested fix

Any of:

1. Seed a default `resolv.conf` into `$SNAP_DATA/etc` from an install hook — e.g. a symlink to `/run/systemd/resolve/stub-resolv.conf`, or a small file with the stub plus a public fallback.
2. Narrow the layout to the specific paths the snap needs under `/etc` rather than binding all of `/etc`.
3. If the current behaviour is intended, document that `$SNAP_DATA/etc/resolv.conf` must be provided by the operator.

Happy to test a fix on Ubuntu Core.

## Still current

Checked against `main`: `charmed-cloudflared-snap/snap/snapcraft.yaml` still carries the `/etc` layout, and `charmed-cloudflared-snap/snap/hooks/configure` only normalises snap options and restarts the service — nothing creates `$SNAP_DATA/etc/resolv.conf`.

items.body:
DHCPv4 supplied my DNS server's IPv4 address, but DHCPv6 ran immediately afterwards and `/etc/resolv.conf` ended up containing only the IPv6 address of the same DNS server. `setup.sh` then disables IPv6 without updating the resolver configuration, leaving the configured DNS server unreachable. After a bunch of `Temporary failure resolving` warnings for security.debian.org and deb.debian.org (step 2/9), followed by `Failed to fetch` errors, the install ultimately failed.
```
Setup failed at line 84.
Installation failed at line 340.
Container 108 was kept for diagnosis. It was not deleted automatically.
```
Jumping into the container, I found the issue. IPv6 was now disabled, but the following (obfuscated real address) was still the only resolver:
```
root@valheim:~# cat /etc/resolv.conf
search lan.
nameserver 1234:5678:abcd::6:66
```

A cleaner fix is to disable IPv6 before the first boot. I tested this modification to `install.sh` with a fresh install and everything went smoothly.

_After this existing code_
```
pct create "$CTID" "$TEMPLATE_STORAGE:vztmpl/$TEMPLATE" \
  --arch "$REQUIRED_ARCH" \
  --ostype debian \
  --hostname "$CT_HOSTNAME" \
  --cores "$CORES" \
  --memory "$MEMORY_MB" \
  --swap "$SWAP_MB" \
  --rootfs "$ROOTFS_STORAGE:$DISK_GB" \
  --net0 "$NET_CONFIG" \
  --unprivileged 1 \
  --features nesting=1 \
  --onboot 1 \
  --start 0
```
My addition
```
info "Configuring IPv4-only networking before first boot"

if ! pct mount "$CTID" >/dev/null; then
  die "Could not mount container $CTID to configure IPv6."
fi

CT_ROOT="/var/lib/lxc/$CTID/rootfs"
IPV6_SYSCTL="$CT_ROOT/etc/sysctl.d/99-valheim-disable-ipv6.conf"

if ! (
  set -e

  mkdir -p "$CT_ROOT/etc/sysctl.d"

  cat >"$IPV6_SYSCTL" <<'EOF'
net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6 = 1
net.ipv6.conf.default.disable_ipv6 = 1
net.ipv6.conf.lo.disable_ipv6 = 1
EOF

  # Preserve the mapped root ownership used by an unprivileged LXC.
  chown --reference="$CT_ROOT/etc" "$IPV6_SYSCTL"
  chmod 0644 "$IPV6_SYSCTL"
); then
  pct unmount "$CTID" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
  die "Could not configure IPv6 disablement inside container $CTID."
fi

pct unmount "$CTID" >/dev/null
```
_Existing code_
```
info "Starting container $CTID"
if ! pct start "$CTID"; then
  die "Container $CTID could not be started. Run 'pct start $CTID --debug' on the Proxmox host for the detailed cause."
fi
```

items.title: Basic Debian13 VPS issue
items.body:
When running script on a Debian13 VPS, it breaks DNS resolution mid-run which results in:
[ERROR] [/root/sergey/xray-gateway-installer/lib/06_xray_core.sh] [xray_install] Не удалось загрузить Xray-инсталлятор

The problem is that is my case installation of resolvconf leaves resolv.conf empty:
cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Dynamic resolv.conf(5) file for glibc resolver(3) generated by resolvconf(8)
#     DO NOT EDIT THIS FILE BY HAND -- YOUR CHANGES WILL BE OVERWRITTEN

After restoring health to DNS script run fine to the end.

Also my Debian13 image was very basic, there wasnt even cron pre-installed, so that broke script too towards the end.

Probably your should account for that happening.

Below is the updated permissions configuration, which minimizes access for the GitHub token. Update your workflow file with this suggested configuration to resolve this issue:

```diff
  name: Agent Capability Tests - ARM
  on: 
    workflow_dispatch:
+ permissions:
+   contents: read
  jobs:
    test-host-outbound:
      runs-on: ARMLinuxRunner
      steps:
        - name: Harden Runner
          uses: step-security/harden-runner@rc

              github.com:443

              github.com:443
              goreleaser.com:443
              production.cloudflare.docker.com:443
```

items.title: DNS issues in user-defined docker networks

labels.name: K8s/Tools
labels.description: Related to container/cloud native  tools, orchestrators

items.body:
The DNS resolution for urunc-based containers which start in a user-defined network of docker does not work. To reproduce the issue:
1. Create a new network in docker.
```
$ sudo docker network create -d bridge my-bridge-network
74bc6ad05c22bdec6267fe95d27b3c3ac13be3bda89c73463890068893bbbaff
```
2. Start a urunc container in this network:
```
$ sudo docker run --rm --network my-bridge-network -it --runtime io.containerd.urunc.v2 harbor.nbfc.io/nubificus/urunc/busybox-qemu-linux-raw:latest
```
3. From inside the container try to resolve any domain:
```
# nslookup github.com
nslookup: write to '127.0.0.11': Connection refused
;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached
```

As shown from nslookup, the DNS request goes to `127.0.0.11`. Also the `/etc/resolv.conf` of the container:
```
# cat /etc/resolv.conf 
# Generated by Docker Engine.
# This file can be edited; Docker Engine will not make further changes once it
# has been modified.

nameserver 127.0.0.11
...
```

This happens because docker sets up an internal DNS server which listens at localhost for each container inside the network namespace (See https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/#dns-services). Therefore, when docker sets the localhost as a DNS server in `/etc/resolv.conf`, a urunc based container does not communicate with the localhost of the network namespace in the host, but with the localhost inside the sandbox and hence the request fails.

items.body:
## GitHub Token Permissions Are Not Set to Minimum in Workflow

### Summary
The GitHub token permissions in your workflow file (.github/workflows/load_tests_int.yml) exceed the minimum required. Reducing permissions to the minimum necessary enhances security by limiting the access scope of the token, thereby lowering the risk of accidental or malicious misuse.

### Why This is Important
Using excessive permissions in GitHub workflows can expose your repository to potential security risks. The GitHub token grants access to repository resources, and any unnecessary permissions increase the likelihood of sensitive actions being performed without justification. By applying the principle of least privilege, you protect your repository from unintended data exposure and ensure that each job only has access to what it absolutely needs.

### Evidence of Excessive Permissions
For more context, please refer to the [build log](https://github.com/step-security/arm-int-tests/actions/runs/11379403105/job/31656791414#step:0:1) from your recent workflow run, which highlights the permissions granted to the GitHub token that exceed the recommended minimum.

### Suggested Fix
Below is the updated permissions configuration, which minimizes access for the GitHub token. Update your workflow file with this suggested configuration to resolve this issue:

```diff
  name: Agent Capability Tests Int
  on: 
    workflow_dispatch:
+ permissions:
+   contents: read
  jobs:
    test-host-outbound:
      runs-on: ubuntu-latest
      steps:
        - name: Harden Runner
          uses: step-security/harden-runner@int-sh
          with:
            egress-policy: audit
            allowed-endpoints: >
              github.com:443
              goreleaser.com:443
              
        
        - run: resolvectl status
        
       
        - run: cat /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf
        - run: cat /etc/resolv.conf
        
        - name: Checkout code
          uses: actions/checkout@v3
        - run: curl www.pastebin.com
        - name: Run outbound calls from host
          run: |
            start_time=$(date +%s)
            end_time=$((start_time + 90))  # 5 minutes = 300 seconds
            
            while [ $(date +%s) -lt $end_time ]; do
              curl -I https://www.google.com
              curl -I https://goreleaser.com
              sleep 10  # wait 10 seconds between calls
            done
    
    test-docker-outbound:
      runs-on: ubuntu-20.04
      steps:
        - name: Harden Runner
          uses: step-security/harden-runner@int-sh
          with:
            egress-policy: block
            allowed-endpoints: >
              archive.ubuntu.com:80
              github.com:443
              goreleaser.com:443
              production.cloudflare.docker.com:443
              *.docker.io:443
              security.ubuntu.com:80
              
        - run: cat /etc/resolv.conf
        - run: cat /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf
      
        - name: Checkout code
          uses: actions/checkout@v3
        - name: Run outbound calls from within Docker container
          continue-on-error: true
          run: |
            # Start the container
            docker run --rm -d --name test-container ubuntu:latest sleep 90
            
            # Install curl in the container
            docker exec test-container apt-get update
            docker exec test-container apt-get install -y curl
            
            # Print /etc/resolv.conf from the container
            docker exec test-container cat /etc/resolv.conf
            
            # Make outbound calls
            for i in {1..9}; do
              docker exec test-container curl -I https://www.google.com
              docker exec test-container curl -I https://goreleaser.com
              sleep 10  # wait 10 seconds between calls
            done
            
            # Stop the container
            docker stop test-container
        - name: Print Docker logs with journalctl
          run: |
              sudo journalctl -u docker.service --no-pager 
          shell: bash
        
        - run: cat /etc/resolv.conf
        - run: cat /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf

      steps:

          uses: step-security/harden-runner@int-sh
          with:
            egress-policy: audit
            allowed-endpoints: >

              auth.docker.io:443
              github.com:443
              goreleaser.com:443
              production.cloudflare.docker.com:443
              registry-1.docker.io:443
              security.ubuntu.com:80

            FROM ubuntu:latest
            RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
            RUN for i in {1..9}; do curl -I https://www.google.com && curl -I https://goreleaser.com; sleep 10; done
            EOF
            
            # Build the Docker image
            docker build -t test-image .
            
            # Print /etc/resolv.conf from the build container (temporary container used during build)
            container_id=$(docker create test-image)
            docker start $container_id
            docker exec $container_id cat /etc/resolv.conf
            docker stop $container_id
            docker rm $container_id

          run: |
              sudo journalctl -u docker.service --no-pager 
          shell: bash
        
        - run: cat /etc/resolv.conf
        - run: cat /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf
    test-long-running-docker:
      runs-on: ubuntu-latest
      steps:
        - name: Harden Runner
          uses: step-security/harden-runner@int-sh
          with:
            egress-policy: block
            allowed-endpoints: >
              archive.ubuntu.com:80
              auth.docker.io:443
              github.com:443
              goreleaser.com:443
              production.cloudflare.docker.com:443
              registry-1.docker.io:443
              security.ubuntu.com:80
              
        - run: cat /etc/resolv.conf
      
        
        - name: Checkout code
          uses: actions/checkout@v3
        - name: Run long-running Docker container with outbound calls
          continue-on-error: true
          run: |
            # Start the long-running container
            docker run --rm -d --name long-running-container ubuntu:latest bash -c "
              apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && 
              while true; do 
                curl -I https://www.google.com; 
                curl -I https://goreleaser.com; 
                sleep 10; 
              done
            "
            
            # Print /etc/resolv.conf from the container
            docker exec long-running-container cat /etc/resolv.conf
            
            # Let the container run for 5 minutes
            sleep 90
            
            # Stop the container
            docker stop long-running-container
        - name: Print Docker logs with journalctl
          run: |
              sudo journalctl -u docker.service --no-pager 
          shell: bash
       
        - run: cat /etc/resolv.conf
        - run: cat /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf
```

### Next Steps
Please review and update the workflow file with these minimum permissions. If additional permissions are necessary for certain steps, specify only those permissions explicitly.

items.title: security(dns): the agent container relies on Docker's embedded resolver; pin a non-forwarding resolver and test DNS exfiltration
items.body:
Part of the containment audit (#109). **Severity: medium** (high until the open checks below are done).

## Finding

The agent container has no `--dns` setting (grep of the repo: no `--dns` flag anywhere), so it gets Docker's embedded resolver, which is configured to forward to the host resolver. From inside a running lea container (lea 0.1.x, Docker host, Ubuntu kernel 7.0.0-38):

```
$ cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 127.0.0.11
search home
options edns0 trust-ad ndots:0
# Based on host file: '/etc/resolv.conf' (internal resolver)
# ExtServers: [host(127.0.0.53)]
```

The nested Podman adds a second path: pasta runs with `--dns-forward 169.254.1.1`, so every nested container's DNS goes to lea's resolver, and from there to the host's.

The agent itself does not need any DNS: it reaches the outside through `HTTP(S)_PROXY=lea-proxy`, and squid resolves names. `tests/proxy/run.sh` covers DNS rebinding at the proxy, but no test checks that **the agent container cannot resolve external names itself**.

Runtime checks done from inside a running lea (2026-10-26):

```
$ getent hosts example.com        # no output: the embedded resolver does not resolve external names
$ curl -m 3 http://169.254.169.254/   # 403 from lea-proxy (private destination refused)
```

So on this host the embedded DNS does **not** answer external names on the `--internal` network. But this is Docker behaviour (it changed across Moby releases), not something lea enforces or tests, and `ExtServers: [host(127.0.0.53)]` shows the forwarder is still configured. Still open: whether queries are forwarded upstream even when no answer comes back (a query name is enough to exfiltrate), TXT/long names, and direct UDP/TCP 53 to public resolvers (`dig` is not in the image).

## Risk

DNS is the classic exfiltration channel that bypasses an HTTP proxy. The OpenAI write-up of 23/10/2026 on containing its training environments names a misconfigured DNS resolver as the leak. A prompt-injected agent could encode data in query names (`<data>.attacker.tld`), and the host resolver would carry it out, without anything in the squid log.

## Proposed fix

- Do not rely on Docker defaults. Start the lea container with a resolver that cannot reach the outside. Two options: point `--dns` at a small resolver on the proxy that answers only `lea-proxy` and the `internal-hosts` names and returns REFUSED/NXDOMAIN for everything else (and logs it), or use `--dns 127.0.0.1` with no local server, so all lookups fail fast.
- Do the same for nested containers (pasta `--dns-forward` target) and keep `NO_PROXY` names resolvable.
- `lea doctor` warns when the agent container can resolve an external name.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Inside lea, `getent hosts example.com` fails (no address), and `curl -m 5 https://example.com` still works through the proxy.
- [ ] Inside lea, a DNS query sent directly to 8.8.8.8:53 and 1.1.1.1:53, over UDP and TCP, times out (`dig` is not in the image: use a small Python probe in the test, or add `bind-utils` to the test image only).
- [ ] A lookup of `aaaa…(60 chars).<decoy-domain> TXT` from inside lea never reaches the decoy authoritative server in `make test-proxy` / `make test-isolation` (assert on the decoy's query log).
- [ ] The same three checks pass from a nested Podman container.
- [ ] Added to `tests/integration/inside-isolation.sh` and run in CI.

items.body:
Hello,

I have witnessed this problem with Discord, but I believe it to be a generic issue.

With `private-etc=resolv.conf`, the jail will receive a copy of the system's resolv.conf. If the system is now moved to a different location/network with a different DNS server, the system's resolv.conf will be updated to use the new server, but the jail's  resolv.conf will not. DNS requests will henceforth fail in the jail as they try to use an unreachable server.

Ideally the jail's resolv.conf should be kept in sync with the system's, but this might require special handling of this file.
Alternatively, the DNS server in the jail's resolv.conf could be set to a globally reachable one instead of the local network's one, such as 1.1.1.1, with `dns=1.1.1.1`. But this unlikely to be in everyone's interest.

**Reproduce**

- `firejail --noprofile --private-etc=resolv.conf bash -c 'while true; do cat /etc/resolv.conf; getent hosts google.com; sleep 5; done'`
- While this runs, move the machine to a different network with different DNS resolver
- -> resolv.conf won't be updated, getent fails.

items.body:
### Nixpkgs version

- Stable (26.05)

### Describe the bug

`virtualisation.podman.defaultNetwork.settings` is turned into a file at `/etc/containers/networks/podman.json`, but the podman packaged in nixpkgs resolves its network config directory to the graph root (`/var/lib/containers/storage/networks`). The file in `/etc` is never read, so the option has no effect and fails silently.

Concretely, even with `dns_enabled = true`, DNS on the default `podman` network is never enabled and `aardvark-dns` is never started.


### Steps to reproduce

1. NixOS config:

```nix
virtualisation.podman = {
  enable = true;
  defaultNetwork.settings.dns_enabled = true;
};
virtualisation.oci-containers = {
  backend = "podman";
  containers.foo = { image = "docker.io/library/alpine"; cmd = [ "sleep" "infinity" ]; };
};
```

2. Rebuild, let the container start, then observe the setting is not applied:

```
$ podman network inspect podman | grep dns_enabled
          "dns_enabled": false,

$ ss -lnup | grep ':53'
# (empty -- aardvark-dns is not running)

$ podman exec foo cat /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 1.1.1.1        # host DNS, not the network gateway
```

3. The file the module writes *does* exist and *does* say `dns_enabled: true`, it is simply not read:

```
$ cat /etc/containers/networks/podman.json
{
  "dns_enabled": true,
  ...
}
```

### Expected behaviour

`virtualisation.podman.defaultNetwork.settings` is applied. For `dns_enabled = true` that means `podman network inspect podman` reports `dns_enabled: true` and `aardvark-dns` listens on the network gateway (`10.88.0.1:53`).

### Screenshots

_No response_

### Relevant log output

```console

```

### Additional context

- A working workaround is to override where podman's network config gets read from:
```nix
virtualisation.containers.containersConf.settings.network.network_config_dir = "/etc/containers/networks";
```
- podman's own documentation states the rootful default network config directory is `/etc/containers/networks`. But here the effective default seems to be `$graphroot/networks` (which the docs describe as the *rootless* default), so either podman's default changed or the nixpkgs build differs -- either way the module's write path no longer matches what the binary reads.
- An alternative fix on the nixpkgs side would be to write the network file to the graph root instead (`$graphroot/networks`).

items.title: apim3 Helm chart: dnsConfig and dnsPolicy cannot be set on component pods
items.body:
## Describe the bug :

The apim3 Helm chart does not expose dnsConfig or dnsPolicy for any component (gateway, management API, portal, console). Values set under these keys are silently ignored: no error, no warning, and nothing is rendered into the pod spec.

As a result, pod DNS options such as ndots cannot be set through the chart. With the Kubernetes default (ndots:5), any backend hostname with fewer than 5 dots is first tried against every cluster search domain before the real name. The gateway's async DNS resolver uses a single nameserver, a 5-second timeout and no retry, so these extra lookups increase the risk of "Failed to resolve" errors, which the gateway returns to clients as HTTP 502.

## To Reproduce :

Steps to reproduce the behaviour:
1. Add the following to the chart values:
gateway:
  deployment:
    dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
    dnsConfig:
      options:
        - name: ndots
          value: "2"
1. Run helm template (or helm install / helm upgrade) with the apim3 chart.
1. Inspect the rendered gateway Deployment, or run "kubectl get deploy <gateway> -o yaml" / "cat /etc/resolv.conf" in a gateway pod.
1. See that neither dnsConfig nor dnsPolicy is present, and the pod still uses ndots:5.

## Expected behaviour :
- gateway.deployment.dnsConfig and gateway.deployment.dnsPolicy (and the equivalents for api, portal and ui) are rendered into the pod spec.
- When these values are not set, the rendered output is identical to today (no default change).
- The setting persists across helm upgrade.
- The options are documented in the chart values reference, with a note that ndots:2 is a sensible value for gateways calling external backends (cluster search domains are kept, so in-cluster short names still resolve).

## Current behaviour :
- The values are silently ignored, so it looks as if they were applied when they were not.
- The only way to set ndots is to patch the Deployment by hand, which the next helm upgrade silently reverts.
- The other workaround, -Dvertx.disableDnsResolver=true, switches to blocking JVM DNS lookups, which can cause latency spikes under load.

## Useful information :
- Chart templates checked: no match for dnsConfig or dnsPolicy in apim3 4.7.6, 4.10.33, 4.11.30 and 4.12.23.
- Measured on a production gateway with packet capture, one lookup of an external 4-dot hostname:
** ndots:5 (default): 5 names queried, 20 NXDOMAIN responses
** ndots:2: 1 name queried, 0 NXDOMAIN responses
- Suggested template change (following the existing hostAliases / topologySpreadConstraints pattern):

items.title: Supervisor diagnostics (Sentry) DNS retry storm saturates Docker's embedded resolver, killing all add-on DNS until reboot
items.body:
### Describe the issue you are experiencing

The Supervisor's diagnostics/crash-reporting (Sentry) feature can take down DNS for **every add-on container** during an upstream DNS outage, and it does not self-heal — a host reboot is required to recover.

When upstream DNS is slow or unreachable, the Supervisor's Sentry client keeps re-resolving its ingest host `o427061.ingest.sentry.io` (A **and** AAAA) with no negative-DNS caching, backoff, or connectivity gating. These lookups accumulate in Docker's embedded resolver (`127.0.0.11`) until it hits its hard **1024 concurrent-query** limit and starts returning `REFUSED` to **all** containers. Add-ons then lose DNS entirely: the Tailscale add-on can't resolve `controlplane.tailscale.com` and falls off the tailnet, CIFS backup mounts time out, `tailscaled` wedges, etc. The Supervisor watchdog is container-level, so nothing restarts and only a reboot recovers.

In my incident this lasted ~16 h. The Sentry endpoint accounted for **2016 of 2052 (98%)** of all failed external DNS lookups in the window (across ~1984 distinct source sockets) — it was clearly the source that saturated the resolver. A best-effort telemetry feature shouldn't be able to exhaust host DNS for the whole system.

### What type of installation are you running?

Home Assistant OS

### Which operating system are you running on?

Home Assistant Operating System

### Steps to reproduce the issue

This was observed in the wild rather than synthetically reproduced, but the mechanism is deterministic given a sustained upstream-DNS failure:

1. HAOS install with diagnostics enabled (the default), so the Supervisor's Sentry client is active (`config.diagnostics: true`). No Core `sentry` integration is needed.
2. Make the host's upstream DNS resolver slow/unreachable while the rest of the network stays up — e.g. the configured/DHCP resolver starts timing out on port 53 (in my case the router at `192.168.1.1`).
3. The Supervisor's Sentry background worker keeps trying to send events, re-resolving `o427061.ingest.sentry.io` (A + AAAA) on each attempt. With no negative-DNS caching/backoff, the failing lookups accumulate in Docker's embedded resolver (`127.0.0.11`).
4. Within ~2 h the resolver hits its limit and logs `[resolver] more than 1024 concurrent queries`, then returns `REFUSED` to every container → all add-ons lose DNS (Tailscale drops off the tailnet, mounts time out, etc.).
5. It does not recover on its own (container-level watchdog sees containers as "running"); a host reboot is required.

### Anything in the Supervisor logs that might be useful for us?

```txt
# From the host journal (`ha host logs`); the Sentry DNS storm surfaces in Docker's embedded resolver, not the Supervisor container log.

# ~2016 failed forwards for the Sentry endpoint (A and AAAA), 02:08–04:15:
dockerd: level=error msg="[resolver] failed to query external DNS server" dns-server="udp:192.168.1.1:53" error="...i/o timeout" question="o427061.ingest.sentry.io. IN AAAA"
dockerd: level=error msg="[resolver] failed to query external DNS server" dns-server="udp:192.168.1.1:53" error="...i/o timeout" question="o427061.ingest.sentry.io. IN A"

# Resolver cap reached at 04:15, then repeated 3602x over ~16h (04:15–20:02):
dockerd: level=error msg="[resolver] more than 1024 concurrent queries"

# Collateral damage — Tailscale add-on wedged, never restarted by the container-level watchdog:
kernel: INFO: task tailscaled:3496 blocked for more than 120 seconds.
dockerd: level=warning msg="Health check for container ... error: OCI runtime exec failed: ... error executing setns process: exit status 1"
```

### System information

```
arch: aarch64
channel: stable
docker: 29.3.1
hassos: "17.3"
homeassistant: 2026.6.3
machine: raspberrypi4-64        # Raspberry Pi 4, 2 GB RAM
operating_system: Home Assistant OS 17.3
state: running
supervisor: 2026.06.1
supported: true
timezone: Europe/Paris
hassio_dns (CoreDNS) plugin: 2026.02.0

# /etc/resolv.conf
nameserver 172.30.32.3        # Supervisor CoreDNS
search local.hass.io
options timeout:10

# Supervisor DNS config AT THE TIME of the incident:
#   servers: []  -> no explicit upstream; relied on the DHCP router (192.168.1.1) + fallback.
# (Since changed to dns://1.1.1.1 + dns://1.0.0.1 as a workaround — see below.)
```

### Additional information

**Root cause (verified in source on `main`):**
- `bootstrap.py` initializes Sentry whenever `config.diagnostics` is set.
- `utils/sentry.py` calls `sentry_sdk.init(dsn="…@o427061.ingest.sentry.io/…", …)` with bare defaults — no transport rate limit, no retry/backoff bound, no negative-DNS caching, and no check that the network or Sentry is reachable.
- `misc/filter.py`'s `before_send` filters only on config/exception type, never on connectivity.

**This is not a Docker bug.** On Docker 29.x the embedded resolver releases query slots correctly and returns `REFUSED` on overload by design (the old slot-leak, [moby#22185](https://github.com/moby/moby/issues/22185), was fixed in 24.0.0). The cap was hit by legitimate, unbounded query volume from the diagnostics client — the fault is the unbounded source.

**Suggested fix** — the diagnostics transport should never be able to exhaust host DNS:
- Gate sends on the Supervisor's existing connectivity signal (skip Sentry sends when known-offline); extend `before_send`/the transport to honor it.
- Bound the transport: rate-limit, cap/abandon retries on transport-level failures, and back off after repeated failures instead of retrying continuously.
- Avoid re-resolving the ingest host on every attempt (cache it); skip AAAA when there's no IPv6 route.

**Workarounds (for affected users):**
- Disable diagnostics: `ha supervisor options --diagnostics=false`.
- Set explicit CoreDNS upstreams instead of relying on the DHCP resolver: `ha dns options --servers dns://1.1.1.1 --servers dns://1.0.0.1 && ha dns restart`.

**Related / prior art:** #4014 and #3973 (Sentry retry storm on blocked/timing-out DNS — same trigger, but neither reaches the resolver-cap cascade / total add-on outage); home-assistant/core#81566 and home-assistant/core#162822 (Sentry DNS-request spam — trigger documented, not the cascade).

A secondary HA OS factor — `/etc/resolv.conf` `options timeout:10`, dual A+AAAA, and no negative caching — amplifies the pileup during an upstream outage and may warrant a separate `operating-system` issue.

items.title: No DNS resolution in NixOS containers if `networking.resolvconf.useLocalResolver = true;`
Guest /etc/resolv.conf does not preserve Kubernetes DNS search domains and resolver options
items.body:
## Environment

- microsandbox: v0.7.10
- Also present in the v0.6.8 guest DNS configuration code
- Linux x86_64, KVM
- microsandbox running inside a Kubernetes Pod
- Debian-based guest with glibc resolver

## Summary

When a microsandbox guest starts, its `/etc/resolv.conf` is regenerated with only the sandbox gateway nameservers.

The Kubernetes Pod's DNS search domains and resolver options (such as `ndots:5`) are not propagated into the guest.

As a result, Kubernetes short service names may fail to resolve, even though their fully qualified domain names (FQDNs) resolve successfully.

## Steps to Reproduce

The following uses fictional service and namespace names.

**1. Start microsandbox inside a Kubernetes Pod.**

The Pod's `/etc/resolv.conf` normally includes entries similar to:

```text
nameserver <cluster-dns-ip>
search demo.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
options ndots:5
```

**2. Create a sandbox with network access to Kubernetes services.**

For example, using a test sandbox:

```bash
msb create python --name repro --net "public,private"
```

**3. Inspect the guest DNS configuration.**

```bash
msb exec repro -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
```

The generated file contains only sandbox gateway nameservers, without the Kubernetes search domains or resolver options.

**4. Compare short-name and FQDN resolution.**

```bash
# Short name
msb exec repro -- getent hosts sample-api

# Fully qualified name
msb exec repro -- getent hosts sample-api.demo.svc.cluster.local
```

The FQDN resolves successfully, while the short name fails.

**5. Restore the search domains manually.**

```bash
msb exec repro -- sh -c \
  'printf "search demo.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local\noptions ndots:5\n" >> /etc/resolv.conf'
```

After this modification, the short service name resolves successfully.

## Expected Behavior

The guest should support standard Kubernetes DNS search-domain resolution without requiring manual modification of `/etc/resolv.conf`.

Using the sandbox gateway as the guest DNS nameserver is expected, as microsandbox intercepts DNS traffic to enforce network policies.

However, DNS search domains and relevant resolver options should be configurable independently.

## Actual Behavior

The guest DNS configuration contains only the sandbox gateway nameservers.

DNS search domains and resolver options from the Kubernetes environment are not propagated.

This prevents applications that rely on Kubernetes short service names from resolving those names automatically.

## Suspected Cause

The guest-side DNS initialization code generates `/etc/resolv.conf` using only the configured nameservers:

```rust
let mut content = String::new();

if let Some(dns) = dns_v4 {
    content.push_str(&format!("nameserver {dns}\n"));
}

if let Some(dns) = dns_v6 {
    content.push_str(&format!("nameserver {dns}\n"));
}
```

Source: [v0.7.10 `crates/agentd/lib/network.rs`](https://github.com/superradcompany/microsandbox/blob/v0.7.10/crates/agentd/lib/network.rs#L568-L588).

The same nameserver-only generation behavior also exists in v0.6.8, so this is not necessarily a new regression introduced in v0.7.10.

## Suggested Improvement

Provide explicit guest DNS resolver configuration options, such as:

- `dns.search_domains`: configurable search suffixes
- `dns.ndots`: configurable resolver `ndots` value
- Optional inheritance of compatible resolver settings from the host environment

The sandbox gateway should remain the configured nameserver to preserve DNS interception and network policy enforcement.

Explicit configuration should be supported so users can avoid unintentionally exposing host-specific DNS search domains to untrusted sandbox workloads.

## Current Workaround

After starting a sandbox, manually append the required search domains and resolver options to the guest's `/etc/resolv.conf`.

This requires an additional initialization step for every sandbox and may need to be repeated when the guest DNS configuration is regenerated.

ClusterFirst | 默认策略，优先通过集群的 DNS 解析 Kubernetes 服务域名，无法解析时退回到宿主机的 DNS 设置。 | 优先解析 *.svc.cluster.local 等 Kubernetes 服务域名。 | 普通工作负载，需访问 Kubernetes 服务域名的 Pod。
ClusterFirstWithHostNet | 专为启用 hostNetwork: true 的 Pod 设计，优先解析 Kubernetes 服务域名。 | 与 ClusterFirst 类似，但适用于主机网络场景。 | 使用主机网络但仍需解析 Kubernetes 服务域名的 Pod。
Default | 完全继承宿主机的 DNS 配置，不解析 Kubernetes 服务域名。 | /etc/resolv.conf 与宿主机一致。 | 不需要解析 Kubernetes 服务域名，需与宿主机共享 DNS 配置的场景。
None | 不继承任何 DNS 配置，完全自定义。 | 必须通过 dnsConfig 自定义 nameservers、搜索域等。 | 需要完全隔离或定制 DNS 配置的 Pod，例如使用外部 DNS 服务。

> [!TIP]
> * 如果未指定 dnsPolicy 且未启用 hostNetwork，默认使用 ClusterFirst。
> * 如果启用了 hostNetwork 且未指定 dnsPolicy，默认使用 ClusterFirstWithHostNet。
> * None 策略需要配置 dnsConfig，否则 Pod 将无法解析任何域名。

items.title: useHostDNS drops every nameserver after the first, and a commented or tab-indented resolv.conf line fails the stage
items.body:
## Summary

With `useHostDNS: true`, the cluster DNS upstream resolvers are taken from the host's `/etc/resolv.conf`, but they are passed to `microk8s enable` separated by whitespace. The `dns` addon takes them as **one comma separated argument**, so everything after the first nameserver is read as a further addon name instead.

On a host with more than one `nameserver` line, which is the normal case for DHCP, CoreDNS is configured with only the first resolver and the rest are silently discarded.

## Where

`scripts/cloudinit/20-microk8s-configure-dns.sh`:

```sh
DNS=$(cat /etc/resolv.conf|grep nameserver|cut -f 2 -d " ")
...
microk8s enable dns:$DNS
```

`$DNS` is unquoted, so the shell word-splits it.

Upstream reads the argument as a comma separated list ([`microk8s-core-addons/addons/dns/enable`](https://github.com/canonical/microk8s-core-addons/blob/main/addons/dns/enable)):

```sh
for ns in ${ARGUMENTS[@]//,/ }; do
```

## Three failure modes, all from that one line

Reproduced by running the script's exact logic against a stub `microk8s` that prints its argv.

**1. More than one nameserver: silent, wrong config.**

`/etc/resolv.conf` with `nameserver 8.8.8.8` and `nameserver 1.1.1.1` produces:

```
microk8s enable dns:8.8.8.8 1.1.1.1
```

`1.1.1.1` is not an addon, so `unprotected_xable` prints `Addon core/1.1.1.1 not found` and `continue`s. No non-zero exit. The stage passes, and the cluster resolves through one upstream instead of two. If that one is the resolver that is unreachable from the pod network, cluster DNS is broken with nothing in the install log to say why.

**2. A commented-out nameserver: hard failure.**

`cut -f 2 -d " "` on `# nameserver 9.9.9.9` returns the literal word `nameserver`:

```
microk8s enable dns:nameserver 8.8.8.8
```

The addon validates each value with `ip route get`, fails with `Your input value (nameserver) is not a valid and reachable IP address` and exits 1, which `microk8s enable` propagates. The stage dies.

**3. A tab-separated nameserver line: same hard failure.**

`nameserver\t1.1.1.1` is valid `resolv.conf` syntax. `cut -d " "` does not split on the tab, so field 2 is again `nameserver`.

## Expected

Every `nameserver` entry in `/etc/resolv.conf`, and only real ones, reaches the addon as a single comma separated argument.

## Fix

Parse the nameservers with a field-aware match anchored on the keyword, join with commas, and quote the expansion. The same normalisation should apply to the explicit `clusterConfiguration.dns` value, which feeds the same unquoted expansion and breaks identically if an operator writes two servers separated by a space.

items.body:
Fixes #1676

## Summary

Adds two new `minikube start` flags that allow users to configure DNS search domains inside the minikube node:

- `--dns-search` (string slice): manually specify DNS search domains
- `--auto-dns-search` (bool): auto-detect and propagate the host's DNS search domains from `/etc/resolv.conf`

Both flags can be combined — auto-detected and manual domains are merged with deduplication.

```bash
minikube start --dns-search=corp.example.com,eng.example.com   # manual
minikube start --auto-dns-search                                # auto-detect from host
minikube start --auto-dns-search --dns-search=extra.corp.com   # combined
```

### Before

No way to propagate DNS search domains into the minikube VM. Users behind corporate firewalls had to manually edit `/etc/resolv.conf` inside the node after every start.

### After

```
$ minikube start --dns-search=corp.example.com
$ minikube ssh -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
search corp.example.com
nameserver 192.168.49.1
```

## How it works

- **VM drivers (kvm2, virtualbox, hyperkit, etc.)**: The kubeadm bootstrapper updates `/etc/resolv.conf` (and `/etc/kubelet-resolv.conf` for K8s v1.25 regression) via `sed` after node provisioning.
- **Container drivers (docker, podman)**: The `KIND_DNS_SEARCH` environment variable is passed to the kicbase entrypoint, which handles resolv.conf configuration at container startup.
- **None driver**: Blocked with a clear error, since modifying the host's `/etc/resolv.conf` directly is unsafe.
- A warning is emitted if any search domain overlaps with the cluster DNS domain (`cluster.local` by default).

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `cmd/minikube/cmd/start.go` | Add `dnsSearchDomains` variable |

items.title: pi resolves through its own dnsmasq, so a dnsmasq outage also breaks pi's recovery path
items.body:
pi serves LAN DNS via dnsmasq (`modules/features/lan-dns.nix`) and also resolves through it:

```
$ ssh pi 'cat /etc/resolv.conf'
search tailcab4c0.ts.net
nameserver 127.0.0.1
nameserver ::1
options edns0 trust-ad
```

So while dnsmasq is down, pi cannot resolve anything — including the names it needs to fix itself.

## Observed

geoclue failed to resolve for ~40 minutes and recovered the moment dnsmasq restarted:

```
19:56:11 pi geoclue[1306]: Failed to query location: Error resolving "api.beacondb.net": Name or service not known
…  every ~5 min  …
20:36:37 pi geoclue[1306]: Failed to query location: Error resolving "api.beacondb.net": Name or service not known
20:37:59 pi dnsmasq[4014]: started, version 2.91
```

geoclue is only the visible symptom (and #811 removes that consumer from pi). The consequential one is the auto-upgrade gate, which resolves `github.com`:

```
rev=$(git ls-remote https://github.com/etrobert/setup.git deploy | cut --fields=1)
```

— `modules/features/auto-upgrade.nix:23`. A dnsmasq outage therefore takes out LAN DNS *and* pi's ability to pull the fix for whatever caused it.

Note the `end0-static` profile does specify `dns = "1.1.1.1;9.9.9.9;"`, but resolvconf puts `127.0.0.1` first, so those never get consulted in practice.

## The decision

Whether this is worth fixing at all is a judgement call — the failure mode needs dnsmasq to be broken *and* the config to be un-rebuildable, and there is always SSH-in-and-fix-it over tailscale. If it is worth fixing, the shape is a fallback resolver that does not depend on pi's own dnsmasq.

Not proposing an implementation; filing so the coupling is written down.

Found while tailing `journalctl -f` on pi.

```
root@mininet-sec-0b98d152622847-56c5bc566f-bj67l:/src/mnsec#

root@mininet-sec-0b98d152622847-56c5bc566f-bj67l:/src/mnsec# 
```

As a consequence, K8sPods that are not isolated cannot use the standard DNS config. The correct behavior should be only change the DNS if the user provides the host params `dns_nameservers ` or `dns_extra_opts ` (in case the user only provides the `dns_extra_opts `, how should we deal with the existing name servers? maybe to simplify we only change if the user provides the `dns_nameservers `)

```
nameserver x.x.x.x
options ndots:5
``` 
